name: Smile training / smile mirror practice
lead: Smile training, or smile mirror practice, refers to deliberately rehearsing a smile, typically in front of a mirror or camera, with the aim of making it look more natural or attractive. No formal protocol or published trial of the practice itself was located for this article.

Related science exists on smile types and on the facial feedback hypothesis, the idea that facial expressions can influence emotional experience. A 2016 multi-lab replication did not reproduce a classic 1988 finding, while a later meta-analysis reported a small effect overall [1][2][3].

paras: Anatomical descriptions distinguish a Duchenne smile, which engages the muscle around the eye as well as the mouth-corner muscles, from a voluntary smile using only the zygomaticus major [3]. Voluntary and spontaneous smiles are reported to run through different cortical pathways, and Duchenne smiles are generally judged more sincere [4]. Practitioners of smile training commonly aim to reproduce eye engagement in deliberate smiles, though sources reviewed here do not document that aim.

A 1988 study by Strack, Martin and Stepper had participants hold a pen in their teeth, inducing a smile-like shape, and found they rated cartoons as funnier [1]. A 2016 registered replication across 17 labs did not find systematic effects, though a later analysis pointed to the presence of a camera as a possible methodological factor [1]. A 2019 meta-analysis of 138 studies reported small but robust effects (d about 0.2) [1]. The article describes only the weak form of the hypothesis as having substantial support [1]. Another encyclopedia summary describes results on forced smiling and mood as small or inconsistent [4].
Smiling is reported to raise perceived likability, approachability and in some summaries competence and trustworthiness, with cultural variation [3][4].
No studies found. Related laboratory research on facial feedback is described above and does not test smile training for appearance.

timeline.event: Strack, Martin and Stepper publish the pen-in-mouth facial feedback study [1].
A 17-lab registered replication report does not find systematic facial feedback effects [1].
A meta-analysis of 138 studies reports a small overall effect [1].

card.summary: Rehearsing your smile in a mirror: free and harmless, but no trials test it for looks.
card.note: Facial feedback research is mixed and does not test attractiveness.

quick.overview:
Smile training means practising a smile, often in a mirror or on camera, to make it look more natural or appealing. It is a behavioural practice with no formal protocol.

No studies have tested it for appearance. Nearby research covers smile types and whether making facial expressions affects mood.
quick.mechanism: People practise controlling facial muscles, for example engaging the eye muscles as in a Duchenne smile. Facial feedback research asks whether expressions feed back on emotion; effects reported are small and contested.
quick.risks: No documented harms were found for the practice itself. Evidence for benefits to attractiveness is absent.
